paragraphs.heading: The biggest fish
paragraphs.text: The whale shark, Rhincodon typus, is the largest known fish alive today. It is a slow-moving carpet shark that feeds by filtering, and the biggest reliably recorded was 18.8 m long. It is the only living species in its genus, Rhincodon, and in its family, Rhincodontidae. Despite the name, it is not a mammal but a fish, and like every shark it is no close relative of whales; the name comes from its looks and great size. For all its bulk it is gentle and poses no real danger to people.

paragraphs.heading: A mouth like a sieve
paragraphs.text: The whale shark is an active filter feeder, feeding mainly on plankton, krill, fish eggs and small fish that swim in schools, like sardines and anchovies. It can push over 6,000 liters of water an hour through sieve-like pads on its gills. Its broad, flat head ends in a huge mouth at the very front, rather than underneath as in many other sharks; one 12.1 m shark had a mouth 1.55 m wide. Inside are more than 300 rows of tiny teeth and 20 filter pads used for feeding, and it has five large pairs of gills.

paragraphs.heading: Following the food
paragraphs.text: Whale sharks roam the open waters of every tropical ocean, mostly between 30°N and 35°S, and they are rarely found in water colder than 21 °C. They migrate thousands of miles to make use of seasonal food. At certain coastal spots, large groups gather to feed at predictable times, including Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, and the coasts of Gujarat and Kerala in India.

paragraphs.heading: Tough skin and healing
paragraphs.text: Its skin is dark grey above and white below, marked with pale spots and stripes in a pattern unique to each shark. The skin can be 15 cm thick and is hard and rough to touch. Even its eyeballs carry dermal denticles, shaped differently from those on its body, and the shark can pull its eyes deep into their sockets; both help shield the eyes from harm. Whale sharks can recover from major injuries, may regrow small parts of their fins, and their spots can form again over an old wound.

paragraphs.heading: Eyes for two worlds
paragraphs.text: Its eyes hold a clever trick. Rhodopsin, the pigment in the retina that sees in dim light, is normally most sensitive to green, but two small changes in the whale shark's version tune it to blue, the light that dominates the deep ocean. One of these changes makes the pigment fragile in warmth, so in warm shallow water the shark switches it off. In the cold, 2,000 m below the surface, it switches it back on, which lets the shark see well at both ends of its wide range of depths.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient, threatened shark
paragraphs.text: Whale sharks are thought to live 80 to 130 years, judging from growth bands in their backbones and the growth of free-swimming sharks. The species was first told apart in 1828, after a 4.6 m whale shark was harpooned in Table Bay, South Africa, and the military doctor Andrew Smith described it the following year. It is one of the oldest shark species still alive, with the earliest fossil teeth dating from the Late Oligocene of South Carolina. Today it is listed as Endangered, because its numbers have fallen by more than half over the last 75 years, mostly through targeted fishing, accidental capture in other fisheries, and collisions with large ships.
